name: Out-Group Homogeneity Bias
description: People tend to see members of an out-group as more alike than members of their own group. 'They are all the same' becomes the default impression more easily than it does for 'us'.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to persona work, moderation policy, safety reviews, hiring/internal tools, and algorithmic segmentation. Treating an out-group as interchangeable can flatten user differences and amplify exclusion or unfair defaults.
myth_risk_note: The core out-group-homogeneity effect is well-established, but several studies (e.g., the ingroup-homogeneity-effect literature) show group status and identity-threat conditions can moderate or even reverse the typical direction under specific circumstances -- a real boundary condition worth noting rather than treating the effect as a simple, universally-directional bias.
prevalence_note: Well known in intergroup-perception and prejudice research, and occasionally relevant in inclusive-design or trust-and-safety practice, but not a routine named concept in general UX reviews.

findings.description: Quattrone and Jones found that people perceive outgroups as less variable and more uniform than their own groups, overgeneralizing from small samples of 'them' more readily than from small samples of 'us'. This is the classic out-group homogeneity pattern.
findings.source_title: The perception of variability within in-groups and out-groups: Implications for the law of small numbers.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
